AFL tribunal live updates: Brisbane's Lachie Neale challenges striking ban ahead of grand final
The Brisbane Lions head to the AFL tribunal to challenge Lachie Neale's ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan, in the hopes of freeing the dual Brownlow medallist for the grand final.

Neale's "gut-punch" on Ginnivan could mean the former Brisbane co-captain has played his last game for the Lions, as the team prepares to face Fremantle on Saturday seeking a second premiership three-peat in club history.
Follow all the proceedings and news in our live blog.

Court option no guarantee for Lions
Assuming Neale’s suspension is upheld, which in my view it absolutely should be, can he take it to the high court and run out the clock? - Stephen
Assuming Neale’s suspension is upheld, which in my view it absolutely should be, can he take it to the high court and run out the clock?
IF (I stress if) the Lions lose tonight's case, then they could take the case to the Supreme Court of Victoria, as the Swans did with Andrew Dunkley in 1996.

They wouldn't be trying to run out the clock, rather they would be seeking an injunction against the decision, stating (no doubt) that Neale would not have natural justice regarding another hearing this week.
In the Dunkley case, the injunction was granted, he played the game (and lost) - and then was given a three-match ban the following week.

Can we just stick to deloberation updates Ando?

EDIT: We are now up to about 257 comments, which is more than our footy record on ABC Sport (the Brayden Maynard Tribunal hearing)
Is it about the law, or the vibe?

It's not just a GF, and Lachie's last game for the Lions. It's the opportunity to lead and participate in a potential 3rd GF legacy. Lachie is a huge part of why this team has been so successful. Blurred vision and pretty minor incident with no harm done. Let him play! - Winter

It's not just a GF, and Lachie's last game for the Lions. It's the opportunity to lead and participate in a potential 3rd GF legacy. Lachie is a huge part of why this team has been so successful. Blurred vision and pretty minor incident with no harm done. Let him play!
- Winter
Winter,
In one sense I can't argue with your points. There is a historic "defining moment" in Lachie Neale's career on the line.
However. He didn't have to run towards Ginnivan (and away from the ball). He didn't have to make contact - he could have yelled something pithy on his way by.

He didn't have to knock him over. I don't see why a leader / veteran of a team in the second-most consequential game of the season (trying to get to the most consequential game of the season) would bring on an incident like this?
It's not a fantastic outcome either way, IMHO.

It's not quite that simple here
Answer the question about the weather, but not: What is the difference between medium and low impact???? - Mark
Answer the question about the weather, but not: What is the difference between medium and low impact????
- Mark
Mark,
Low impact is for low force or minimal contact where the player gets up quickly.
Medium impact is for greater force OR off-the-ball incidents.

So Neale's team is arguing it's minimal force, and Ginnivan wasn't injured and got up straight away. The AFL is arguing that it was enough to knock him over, and the potential to injure is there AND it's off-the-ball.

Tribunal cases involve two sides of the argument
So Woods says it is a clear strike, Anderson says the vision is inconclusive. It’s two very different takes on what happened. - Tracey
So Woods says it is a clear strike, Anderson says the vision is inconclusive. It’s two very different takes on what happened.
- Tracey
Tracey,
The two legal teams are representing their respective clients, the AFL and Lachie Neale.
It stands to reason that if the charge is contested, there is going to be a difference of opinion on what happened.

If it was completely cut and dried, the Lions would have pleaded guilty and thrown themselves on the mercy of the Tribunal, so to speak, focusing purely on the exceptional and compelling circumstances argument.
What happens now
What's the process once the tribunal comes back please? Do they tend to announce their decision and then explain, just announce or walk through their thinking then announce the decision? - T-Bird
What's the process once the tribunal comes back please? Do they tend to announce their decision and then explain, just announce or walk through their thinking then announce the decision?
- T-Bird
T-Bird,
If and when the Tribunal returns with a verdict, Jeff Gleeson KC will summarise the case and give a verdict, pointing to the basic reasons for the decision.
Then depending on the outcome we get the question of whether there is an appeal or not. We may not get an indication of that tonight.
No reading of the tea leaves
Deliberations have been going for 20 minutes or so.
It hasn't been an instant return, which probably would have meant a fine/all clear for Neale.
But the fact it's gone longer than 5-10 minutes does not of itself mean anything.

There is the argument on whether it actually was an intentional strike, then whether it was sufficient to warrant a week, and then the question of whether there is a get out of suspension card for Neale.
It's hard to ignore the headline act of the grand final. Andrew Woods KC from the AFL asked the Tribunal to consider this as if it were round one. But it's not.
Can they get beyond the "gravity of the consequences" for Neale, which are arguably well above a simple week off?
Will everything be a fine for Lachie Neale
They will find Neale guilty but downgrade it to a fine. This tells kids hitting is wrong , allows for Neale’s ‘unicorn’ status but still punishes him , and all the AFL problems are covered. - Phillip
They will find Neale guilty but downgrade it to a fine. This tells kids hitting is wrong , allows for Neale’s ‘unicorn’ status but still punishes him , and all the AFL problems are covered.

Phillip,

I'm not sure. Some of the evidence points to the least-nasty outcome for the Brisbane star ... but the issue raised about the deterrent factor of the "gut punch" guideliness wasn't really answered by Adrian Anderson.

The jury is out (on whether Brisbane would challenge this in court)
If the verdict is upheld, will the Lions head to court? - Craig Connelly
If the verdict is upheld, will the Lions head to court?

Is it worth it, if they do lose tonight? Who knows. The stakes are pretty high, and there would no doubt be a decent chance they rolled the dice.
Key Event
A summary of where we are
The AFL (and the Tribunal chair agrees) that the incident was off the ball and not in play.
The league says it was a clear swinging arm, not a football act, and that it meets the definition of a strike.
The AFL says Neale had time to decide what to do, and decided to make contact.
Neale's lawyers say it wasn't a strike but a bump or a body-check, and according to Lachie Neale he spoke to Jack Ginnivan today and the Hawks star agreed.
The argument is that if it is a strike, it's of negligble impact, Ginnivan got up and ran away and was not treated or needed treatment off-field.
They say if this is all rejected, we get to the exceptional and compelling circumstances, including the fact that Neale is days away from what could be the "defining moment of his career".
Not to mention his lack of suspensions in a long-and award-filled career.
The fact chair Jeff Gleeson KC essentially compared Neale to a unicorn must go in the Lions player's favour.
